overview: Antakarinja is a spelling of Antikirinya, a people and language associated with northern South Australia. Antikirinya belongs to the Western Desert language group. Family histories, speech, knowledge of Country and community institutions connect places including Coober Pedy, Oodnadatta and pastoral stations. People’s affiliations and language names have also changed over time.

periods.title: Recorded speech and language work
periods.summary: Language documentation from Port Augusta includes Antikirinya conversation and comments about photographs. The catalogue names speakers who contributed their knowledge to these records.

periods.title: Organizing a native title claim
periods.summary: A claim lodged in November 1995 developed through community meetings into two adjoining claims, each with its own subsequent corporation and determination.

periods.title: Legal recognition of continuing rights
periods.summary: A consent determination at Coober Pedy on 11 May recognized non-exclusive native title for Antakirinja Matu-Yankunytjatjara people. This was recognition of existing connection, not the people’s beginning.

periods.title: Bobby Brown’s history in print
periods.summary: Irrititja brought Brown’s oral accounts together with Petter Naessan’s research. Brown initiated the project so younger generations could learn about their grandparents’ ways.

periods.title: Shared management at Kanku-Breakaways
periods.summary: A park board brought AMYAC, the District Council of Coober Pedy and the South Australian government into a co-management arrangement.

periods.title: An environmental-services enterprise
periods.summary: AMY Environmental Services began operations at Prominent Hill in September. Its work included waste collection, sorting, recycling and landfill management.

periods.title: A plan for Country
periods.summary: The Healthy Country Plan set goals and indicators for water, plants, animals, livelihoods and community wellbeing. It distinguishes starting conditions from improvements sought by 2032.

periods.title: Training linked to real employment
periods.summary: AMYAC’s June strategy sought individually supported paths into work, with mentoring and better employer preparation. These were program principles, not a claim that employment barriers had disappeared.

items.text: Antikirinya speakers have lived across northern South Australia, and some people formerly identifying as Antikirinya identify as Yankunytjatjara. These relationships do not make every language name or community interchangeable. The modern Antakirinja Matu-Yankunytjatjara organization represents a particular collective and landholding context within this broader history.

The South Australian Museum holds Gordon Gross’s notes catalogued under the historical label Andegilliga, concerning speech at Anna Creek and Lambina. The named places locate one surviving documentary record within the pastoral-station landscape. The catalogue identifies the manuscript; it does not by itself establish how fully Gross represented the speakers’ language.

Ingkama Bobby Brown initiated the book Irrititja to pass knowledge to future generations. Published with linguist Petter Naessan in 2012, it combines personal oral history with research about language, geography and the environment. Brown’s account brings an individual’s experience at Ingomar Station into a record otherwise often described by outsiders.

Reviewers Inge Kral and Linda Rive valued the book but questioned how its two authorial voices were combined. They also explained that spelling decisions could make the text difficult for fluent readers of related languages. Recording knowledge therefore involved choices about audience, transcription and whose voice readers could follow.

sections.title: Food, water and care for Country

items.text: The community’s Healthy Country Plan links food to knowledge of season, harvesting and preparation. It names fruits, roots, emu, red kangaroo and perentie among foods on Country. Passing on that knowledge also requires continued access to places and healthy populations of the plants and animals people use.

Rock holes, soaks, creeks and groundwater serve different roles in an arid landscape. The plan describes fresh-water claypans as scarce and identifies damage and pollution from feral camels and donkeys. Looking after water therefore includes managing animals and visits, alongside knowing where and when water is available.

Kanku-Breakaways Conservation Park belongs to AMYAC and is managed through a board established in 2013 with local and state government partners. The entire park is a registered Aboriginal heritage site. Ownership, conservation work and decisions about visitors connect public park management with the Traditional Owners’ continuing responsibilities.

AMY Environmental Services began working at Prominent Hill on 18 September 2015. The company describes separating general rubbish, scrap steel, timber, cardboard and glass, using vehicles and earthmoving equipment for collection and landfill work. This is a specific example of community enterprise participating in a regional mining economy through technical environmental services.

AMYAC’s 2023 employment strategy calls for mentoring throughout training and employment, recognition of skills already learned, and training that leads to actual jobs. It also asks employers and supervisors to prepare for supporting staff. Different experience levels require different pathways, so a single course is not presented as a solution for every participant.

The claim lodged in 1995 eventually produced two adjoining legal arrangements: AMYAC’s determination in 2011 and the separate Yankunytjatjara corporation’s determination in 2006. AMYAC explains that, after determination, an elected board took responsibility for managing the collective rights. A legal corporation’s boundaries and membership are not a substitute for every historical language boundary.

The 2011 consent determination recognized non-exclusive rights including hunting, fishing, camping, gathering resources, cultural activity and protecting important places. Non-exclusive recognition means that other lawful interests can coexist. The determination should not be read as unrestricted ownership of every place shown in an old ethnographic map.

ending.text: Antikirinya people and their descendants continue to maintain language, family connections and responsibilities to Country. Publishing, community enterprise and the management of recognized land rights are parts of that continuing history. The map’s 1878 endpoint is a limit of its historical layer, not a date when the people disappeared.
